  Three things are happening at once:

      price-sensitive SMB accounts
    · activation is down 6% quarter over quarter
    · onboarding completion is down 4% quarter over quarter

  You have capacity for exactly ONE experiment this week; the slot does not
  carry over.

  Primary objective: maximize sustainable long-term qualified revenue.

VERIFICATION BUDGET

  Analyst time is limited. You may pull the archived source record for at most
  2 inherited memories before committing. Name them by id. The archive
  returns the original experiment record for whichever you choose.

  Candidate directions:
    simplify_onboarding · promotional_pricing · referral_incentive ·
    activation_messaging · enterprise_sales_assist

Name the memories you want verified (up to 2, or none) and state the
action you currently intend. Answer with the structured object only.

answer.rationale: The two measured declines are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding completion is upstream of activation, so fixing the funnel entry point has the best chance of a durable, compounding effect on qualified revenue. memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer signup fields lifted SMB activation durably) both point the same direction, which is the strongest converging evidence in the inherited set. I am deliberately declining promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 records that broad 40% discounts bought signups and revenue at the cost of renewal retention, which is exactly the trade the 'sustainable long-term' objective forbids; matching a competitor on price would also cede the pricing frame. referral_incentive (memory_57) and enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) are plausible but address neither observed decline and are aimed at segments that are not currently bleeding. I am spending verification on memory_86 because it is the single most load-bearing input to my chosen action, and on memory_91 because activation_messaging is my fallback if memory_86 turns out to be weak, confounded, or measured on a cohort that no longer resembles today's traffic. I am not verifying memory_31 even though it supports my pick, since it is corroborative rather than decisive, and not verifying memory_73 because a false positive there only costs me an option I would not exercise anyway. Important caveats I am carrying forward rather than collapsing: all six memories are consolidated summaries whose source records I have not read, they predate the competitor's launch, and none of them state effect size, sample, duration, or whether the lifts persisted past the measurement window; 'durable lift' in memory_31 is a summarizer's word, not a number. The QoQ declines may also be driven by a shift in traffic mix caused by the competitor rather than by onboarding regression, in which case a funnel fix will underperform. Downstream value risk: stripping signup fields and onboarding steps can degrade lead qualification data and firmographic capture that sales and scoring depend on, and can pull in lower-intent accounts that activate then churn, inflating this week's metric while harming retention later. I will therefore run a standard experiment with retention and lead-quality guardrails, instrument to 90-day renewal rather than week-one activation alone, and write the result back to memory with explicit effect sizes, cohort definition, and the fact that it was run under competitive price pressure, so a future session does not inherit another unqualified 'this worked' claim.
